specPoints.text: practical: investigate the role of anaerobic respiration by yeast in different conditions

primer.text: Yeast can ferment sugar without a breath of oxygen, and that trick fills bakeries and breweries. This practical measures fermentation rate as bubbles of carbon dioxide, varies the water-bath temperature, and closes with a CORMS evaluation that pins down every variable a fair test needs.

lessons.title: Fermentation: Respiration Without Air
sourceHeadings: Practical: investigating anaerobic respiration in yeast
lessons.opening: When oxygen is absent, yeast breaks glucose down into ethanol and carbon dioxide, a pathway called fermentation. The carbon dioxide raises bread dough and the ethanol fills drinks barrels, and both products trace back to the same enzyme-driven anaerobic chemistry this practical measures.
keyPoints: Yeast respires anaerobically by splitting glucose in the absence of oxygen.
The products of that pathway are ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells is known as fermentation.
Bread making relies on carbon dioxide to raise dough, and alcoholic drinks rely on ethanol.
The rate of fermentation can be followed by timing how quickly carbon dioxide appears.

low.restatement: No oxygen? Yeast still eats sugar and gives off alcohol and bubbles.
low.analogy: A back-up generator: not the main power route, but it keeps the lights on when the mains fail.
low.examPointer: Name both products — ethanol and carbon dioxide — and the word fermentation for the definition mark.

medium.restatement: Under anaerobic conditions yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide; this pathway is fermentation, and its commercial weight sits in bread rising and alcoholic drink production, with the reaction rate measurable through carbon dioxide output.
medium.analogy: A yeast cell in a sealed jar is a tiny brewery and bakery sharing one production line.
medium.examPointer: Say anaerobic respiration explicitly before fermentation — examiners want the process named, not only the label.

check.stem: Which products leave yeast glucose when oxygen is absent?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Lactic acid belongs to muscle, not yeast.
Those are inputs of aerobic respiration, not outputs here.
Neither features in respiration products.

check.stem: What is the name of anaerobic respiration carried out by yeast?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Photosynthesis builds glucose using light.
Aerobic respiration requires oxygen.
Distillation is a separation process, not respiration.

check.stem: Why does bread dough rise during fermentation?

options.text: Carbon dioxide released by yeast becomes trapped in the dough
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Ethanol evaporates and pushes the dough up
options.explanation: Ethanol contributes no lift.

options.text: The dough absorbs air from stirring
options.explanation: Rising comes from gas produced in place.
Cell swelling is not the mechanism.

check.stem: Which industry depends directly on the ethanol from fermentation?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Cheese relies on bacteria, not ethanol.
Refining is physical chemistry, not fermentation.
Bread needs the carbon dioxide, and ethanol evaporates away.

check.stem: Why can a sealed sugar solution still support yeast respiration?

options.text: Because yeast can respire without oxygen when glucose is available
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because sealed jars leak oxygen slowly
options.explanation: The pathway needs no oxygen at all.

options.text: Because sugar releases oxygen when wet
options.explanation: Dissolving sugar makes no oxygen.

options.text: Because yeast photosynthesises in the dark
options.explanation: Yeast is a fungus and never photosynthesises.

check.stem: State the word equation products when yeast ferments glucose.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide during anaerobic respiration in yeast.

check.stem: Name the process yeast cells use to respire without oxygen.
check.modelAnswer: Yeast cells respire anaerobically, and the process is called fermentation.

check.stem: Explain why fermentation is described as economically important.
check.modelAnswer: Fermentation underpins two major industries at once, since carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise and ethanol forms the alcohol in drinks, so the same pathway earns money in bakeries and breweries.

check.stem: A brewer finds her fermenting vat stopped bubbling. Suggest one cause tied to this pathway.
check.modelAnswer: The glucose supply may be exhausted, because fermentation needs sugar to continue producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Building the Bubble Counter
lessons.opening: The apparatus is simple and telling: yeast and sugar solution sit in one tube sealed under oil, a capillary tube carries their carbon dioxide into limewater, and a warm water bath sets the pace. Counting bubbles in a fixed interval turns invisible fermentation into data.
keyPoints: Yeast and sugar solution are combined in a boiling tube, the sugar supplying glucose for respiration.
A layer of oil is floated on top to keep oxygen out of the mixture.
A capillary tube links the yeast tube to a second boiling tube holding limewater.
The yeast tube stands in a water bath at a chosen temperature.
Bubbles delivered in a fixed period, such as two minutes, are counted as the measure of rate.
The bath temperature is then changed and the count repeated.

low.restatement: Yeast plus sugar in a tube, oil cap on top, tube to limewater, sit it in warm water, count the bubbles.
low.analogy: A fizzy drink with a straw into a cloudy glass — the straw delivers the fizz, the glass proves it is carbon dioxide.
low.examPointer: Say why the oil matters: it blocks oxygen so only anaerobic respiration proceeds.

medium.restatement: Yeast suspended in sugar solution provides the glucose substrate; oil layered above excludes oxygen so the culture respires anaerobically; a capillary tube feeds the released gas into limewater, and bubbles counted per timed interval in a temperature-controlled water bath give the rate of fermentation.
medium.analogy: A sealed kitchen where the chef (yeast) can only cook one recipe, and every plate leaving the kitchen is counted at the door.
medium.examPointer: Quote the fixed timing window — for instance two minutes — because fair comparisons need equal counting periods.

check.stem: Why is a layer of oil added above the yeast mixture?

options.text: To stop oxygen entering, forcing anaerobic respiration
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: To feed the yeast extra energy
options.explanation: Oil is not a yeast food here.

options.text: To colour the solution for counting
options.explanation: Counting uses bubbles, not colour.
The water bath controls temperature.

check.stem: What does the sugar solution contribute to the investigation?

options.text: Glucose that yeast respires during the reaction
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The design excludes oxygen deliberately.
Ethanol is a product, never an input.
Rate is counted, not colour-judged.

check.stem: Which piece of equipment connects the yeast tube to the limewater tube?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Funnels pour liquids, not gases.
Thermometers read temperature.
Filter paper does not carry gas.

check.stem: How is the rate of fermentation measured in this practical?

options.text: Counting the bubbles produced within a fixed time window
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Weighing the tube before and after
options.explanation: Mass loss is not the taught measure.

options.text: Timing how long the limewater clears
options.explanation: Clearing time is not counted.
Ethanol is not measured in this setup.

check.stem: What does limewater confirm about the gas being produced?

options.text: That the bubbles are carbon dioxide, which turns limewater cloudy
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Oxygen leaves limewater unchanged.

options.text: That the gas is ethanol vapour
options.explanation: Ethanol vapour is not the tested gas.
Nitrogen does not cloud limewater.

check.stem: State why oil floats on the sugar solution in this practical.
check.modelAnswer: The oil layer prevents oxygen from entering, so the yeast respires anaerobically.

check.stem: Name the solution that tests for carbon dioxide in the second tube.
check.modelAnswer: Limewater fills the second tube and turns cloudy when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.

check.stem: Explain why the water bath temperature must be set and held steady.
check.modelAnswer: Temperature changes enzyme activity, so a fixed bath temperature isolates it as the variable being tested while keeping every other condition constant.

check.stem: A student's bubbles stop after five minutes at high temperature. Give the likely reason.
check.modelAnswer: The enzymes in the yeast have denatured beyond their optimum, so fermentation halts and carbon dioxide production stops.

lessons.title: Reading the Results, Judging the Test
lessons.opening: More bubbles signal faster fermentation, and warmer water usually brings more bubbles until the yeast enzymes pass their optimum and stall. A CORMS frame then audits the design: the changed factor, the fixed organism, repeated trials, the two measurements, and everything held constant.
keyPoints: Comparing counts across temperatures reveals where yeast respires fastest.
Higher temperatures bring more bubbles while enzymes approach their optimum activity.
Beyond the optimum, denaturation slows carbon dioxide output until it stops.

CORMS: the changed input is temperature, the organism stays the same yeast species, repeats make results reliable, the measure is bubble number over a timed period, and sugar concentration, volume and pH plus yeast mass are controlled.

low.restatement: Count bubbles at each temperature: warmer means more, until too hot kills the enzymes and the fizzing stops.
low.analogy: Tuning an engine — more throttle helps until the pistons overheat and seize.
low.examPointer: Spell out CORMS letters with one clause each; partial CORMS answers lose the evaluation marks.

medium.restatement: Bubble counts rise with bath temperature as enzymes near optimum activity, then fall and stop once denaturation sets in; the evaluation fixes temperature as the changed variable, keeps the yeast species constant, repeats each reading, measures bubbles per timed interval, and controls sugar concentration, volume, pH and yeast mass.
medium.analogy: A taste test where one ingredient changes at a time, the same kitchen and chef cook each round, and every round is judged twice for fairness.
medium.examPointer: Mention reliability through repeats — that single word converts an ordinary evaluation into a full one.

check.stem: What pattern of bubble counts shows yeast respiration speeding up?

options.text: Counts rise as the water bath warms towards the enzymes' optimum
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Falling counts indicate denaturation setting in.

options.text: Counts stay flat at all temperatures
options.explanation: Temperature clearly changes the rate.
Cooling slows enzyme activity.

check.stem: Why does carbon dioxide production stop when the bath runs too hot?

options.text: The yeast enzymes denature beyond their optimum temperature
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The yeast runs out of bubbles to recycle
options.explanation: Bubbles are products, not reserves.
Limewater changes only when gas reaches it.
Oil behaviour is not the cause.

check.stem: In the CORMS frame, which letter covers repeating each temperature?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
C covers temperature, the factor changed.
M covers bubble number and timing.
S covers the controlled quantities.

check.stem: Which quantities belong in the controlled column of this investigation?

options.text: Sugar concentration, solution volume, pH and the mass of yeast added
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Temperature is the changed variable.
The timed window is fixed by design, not varied.
The organism is kept the same, a fixed choice.

check.stem: A class repeats each temperature three times and averages the counts. Which evaluation letter does that strengthen?

options.text: R, because repeated readings make the results reliable
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The organism stayed the same; repeats are reliability.
The measure stayed bubbles per window.
Temperature is the intended independent variable.

check.stem: State what is measured and over what period in this practical.
check.modelAnswer: The number of bubbles produced is counted in a fixed time period such as two minutes.

check.stem: Name the variable that is changed between repeats in this investigation.
check.modelAnswer: The temperature of the water bath is changed for each repeat of the practical.

check.stem: Explain why the same species of yeast must be used at every temperature.
check.modelAnswer: Different yeast strains carry different enzyme optima, so switching species would confound the temperature effect and break the fairness of the comparison.

check.stem: A baker wants maximum dough rise without killing the yeast. Use the results pattern to advise.
check.modelAnswer: Choose a warm setting near the yeast optimum, because bubble output peaks there, and avoid hotter settings where denaturation halts carbon dioxide production.

glossary.definition: Anaerobic respiration carried out by yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The clear liquid that turns cloudy when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.
The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest.
